Evolutionary Microbiology

Kathryn Herr, Ph.D.

Researcher in insect–microbe symbiosis

  • NIH IRACDA FIRST Postdoctoral Teaching Fellow, Emory University (2024–25)
  • Ph.D. Microbiology, Cornell University
  • Based in Bath, UK · right to work in the UK (High Potential Individual visa)

I study how microbes and the plants and animals that host them shape one another, from fluorescent bacteria that influence aphid behaviour to the yeasts that travel with a burying beetle. I combine fieldwork, microbiology, and bioinformatics to ask evolutionary questions about everyday symbioses. Alongside that research I teach undergraduate biology and microbiology, and supervise students through research projects of their own.

Research

How do microbes and their animal or plant hosts shape one another over evolutionary time?

Phyllosphere Pseudomonas and aphid behaviour

Pseudomonas spp. · pea aphids

Leaf surfaces carry dense and variable bacterial communities, and the insects feeding there meet those microbes first. For my dissertation I tested how common fluorescent Pseudomonas from the phyllosphere affect aphid behaviour. Different bacterial strains changed that behaviour in substantially different ways, which matters for how these everyday, non-obligate symbioses evolve.

Burying beetles and their Yarrowia symbionts

Nicrophorus spp. · Yarrowia-like yeasts

Burying beetles (Nicrophorus spp.) locate, bury and preserve small vertebrate carcasses, and carry yeast symbionts with them while they do it. Sampling wild populations in the Adirondack Mountains, I examined how diverse these Yarrowia-like yeasts are across beetle species and what their evolutionary history says about how the association is maintained.

Caulobacter exopolysaccharide and phage defence

Caulobacter crescentus · bacteriophage

Caulobacter crescentus secretes an extracellular polysaccharide layer that prevents bacteriophage from binding to the cell. Using confocal microscopy, fluorescent proteins and plaque assays, I measured that layer across diverse strains and how well each resisted infection. Strains investing more in exopolysaccharide grew more slowly, a trade-off between protection and proliferation.

Study systems

Teaching

  • BIO306: Principles of Microbiology

    2025
    Instructor · Morehouse College

    Co-taught this established upper-level course and redesigned parts of it to bring in more active learning and student-centred work, including spreading assessment across more and smaller assignments to make the course more accessible. Wrote, marked and built rubrics for seven assignments, a group project and four unit exams. Taught the unit on microbial interactions and applied microbiology on my own, co-taught the unit on microbial history and cell structure, and held weekly in-person and online office hours.

  • BIOMI 6300: Computational Approaches for Microbial Systems

    2023
    Guest Instructor · Cornell University

    Designed learning outcomes and built a case study from my own research to teach upper-level bioinformatic analysis of next-generation sequencing data, using active learning (think-pair-share, live polling) to explore trade-offs between genomic and metagenomic, shallow and deep sequencing.

  • Software Carpentry Workshop

Mentoring

I have advised and supported seven undergraduate researchers through independent projects: three over six years in the Hendry Lab at Cornell, three summer researchers on the Microbial Friends and Foes REU, and an honours research student during my postdoc at Emory. Mentoring is one of the most rewarding parts of the job, and it shapes how I teach.
